content.thinking:
I'm planning out a chopper motorbike model in an Overwatch-inspired aesthetic—bold polished sci-fi shapes with bevels, panel lines, dark gunmetal body, and a glowing orange accent. I'm thinking through the construction approach using basic geometric parts and rods, structuring the joint hierarchy starting from the frame through the steering fork and wheel hinges.

Working out sizing: roughly 2.4m length, 1.1m height, with torus-shaped tires oriented along the X-axis using directional parameters, and setting up helper functions for boxes and rods to build the frame rigidly through bone-bound parts.

I'm settling on a limited flat-color palette — gunmetal, orange, chrome, steel, black, rubber, leather, and a cyan glow accent — and planning to paint the tank with an orange base plus a contrasting stripe.

For the tank shape I'm thinking of a loft along the z-axis with teardrop-shaped elliptical cross-sections from rear to front, then applying a custom paint function to add a white center stripe and cyan pinstripes along the edges. Now I'm laying out the vehicle in z-forward, y-up coordinates starting with the rear wheel's position and tire torus dimensions.

Still working out wheel geometry... now figuring out the front wheel's thinner torus and position, then computing the raked fork angle from the steering head down to the front axle.

Fork bottom lands at the axle giving a fork length around 1.16, reasonably long but fine for a chopper look. Now I'm placing the steering joint near the triple tree, aiming it toward the axle so its bone axis runs along the fork direction, with the handlebars and front wheel joint attached as children of that steer joint.

Working out the frame geometry next: I'm computing head tube endpoints by offsetting from the head point perpendicular to the fork axis, getting top around (y1.16, z0.45) and bottom around (y0.94, z0.65), then starting to lay out the top tube from the head tube's upper point.

Continuing with the down tube to the engine bracket, then placing a V-twin engine with angled front and rear cylinders and cooling fins styled in gunmetal with orange and cyan accents, and positioning a low solo seat near the rear wheel.

Adding the final loft station, giving the seat cushion leather-grain paint with stitched edges and a bobber backing plate. Now I'm positioning the tank above the top tube, adjusting its height and center so it sits naturally rather than floating too high, which means tweaking the top tube's endpoints too.

Checking tank proportions along its length with several width/height stations front to back, making sure the nose tucks near the head tube. Noting the seat sits noticeably lower than the tank in this chopper stance, and now sketching the hardtail frame running from the top tube back to the rear axle area.

Then I'm planning the rest of the build out: hardtail chain/seat stays to the rear axle hinge joint, rear fender with glowing tail light, dual exhaust pipes with chrome heat shields on the right side, sissy bar, kickstand hinge, tall ape-hanger handlebars, a glowing headlight and front fender, and brake disc/caliper details, considering mag-style solid hub wheels with glow rings instead of traditional spokes.

Now I'm designing each wheel with 12 radial rods for spokes plus a flat disc rotor, and adding an Overwatch-style accent with a cyan underglow strip along the frame bottom and thin glowing cyan torus rings on the rim sides, using glow-enabled parts for the effect. I'm setting up the wheel joints aligned along the axle axis as hinges so they can spin, and starting to write a makeWheel helper function.

Writing wheel builder code...

Still importing types and defining helper builders...

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy, starting with the root "frame" joint at its world position, then adding a "steer" joint parented to frame with its own offset.

Still writing joint definitions...

I need to add control joints too — a footbrake pedal hinge, clutch lever, and brake lever — keeping it to two hand levers plus one pedal for simplicity. Checking floor clearance, both wheel bottoms sit right at y=0 as expected, and the stowed kickstand and footpegs clear above the ground fine.

For the torus geometry, I'm confirming the segment counts place vertices correctly at the bottom and outer edges so the tire sits flush without gaps. For tread detail, I'm positioning small rubber tread blocks around the wheel's circumference using angle-based coordinates in the wheel's plane.

To orient each tread block to lie flush against the tire's curved surface, I'm working out the rotation math: rotating a box around the X axis by (π/2 - θ) aligns its local radial direction with the correct point on the circle, then translating it to position on the outer radius before merging into the tire geometry.

I need the lugs to sit proud of the crown without poking through the floor plane, so I'm checking the radial math: with tube radius plus lug height, the lug bottoms land a tiny fraction below the wheel's nominal ground line, well under the 2% tolerance. I'll adjust the rear wheel center height so the lugs just kiss the floor, keeping the lowest contact point exactly at y=0.

Setting rear axle cy to 0.372 and front axle cy to 0.352 so the lug tips touch the ground plane cleanly, then updating the fork geometry to match the new front axle position. Now I'm writing the wheel-building function that generates the tire torus, rim, and lug geometry parametrically.

Still defining wheel geometry...

18 rods total. Now I'm adding disc brake rotors as lathed annulus rings (steel-colored, with caliper boxes at the fork) for front and rear wheels, then moving on to shaping the curved front fender sweep.

Working out the fender arc geometry attached to the fork so it turns with steering, computing the angular sweep behind the wheel's top point...

The rotation checks out, confirming the arc sweeps correctly toward the top. Now I'm planning the fender geometry as a box-section sweep along that arc, tapering the radius with a thin, wide profile and flat caps, colored orange for the paint.

For the rear fender I'm figuring out the right starting angle so the arc sweeps from the front-top around the back correctly rather than in reverse.

I should also check whether the rear fender's span clashes with the seat position near the back of the frame.

Adjusting the fender to start around θ=80° keeps it clear of the seat, with the fender trailing edge wrapping to roughly 185°, well below the seat height so it looks properly sloped underneath.

Now I'm moving on to the frame tubes, starting with the head tube as a rod running from the head's bottom to top.

Working out the top tube geometry connecting the head tube to the seat post area, placing it above where the tank would sit, then defining the hardtail rear triangle -- seat stays running from the seat post top down to the rear axle, chain stays from the bottom bracket area to the axle, and a down tube dropping from the head tube base toward the bottom bracket.

Now I'm positioning the engine: a crankcase block sitting central and low, with a V-twin layout -- front cylinder angled forward about 30 degrees, rear cylinder angled backward, each built as a stack of cooling fin discs along their length.

I'm checking for clearance issues between the down tube and the tilted front cylinder near the head, so I'm reducing the tilt to 25 degrees and shortening the cylinder slightly to avoid them touching.

Now I'm laying out the fin stacks oriented along a direction vector, positioning an orange cylinder cover with a cyan glow disk on the left side, and placing a gearbox box behind the engine before moving to the exhaust layout on the right.

For the exhaust, I'm plotting a chrome pipe sweep that curves from the front cylinder port down and back along the right side, defining a series of control points to shape the pipe's path while keeping it clear of the rear wheel and setting a thin tube radius for a realistic look.

I'm adding a chrome flared tip to the exhaust end using a tapered cylinder shape, then moving on to the handlebars—setting up the triple tree and risers at the fork top, with ape hanger grips positioned high and wide, built from a catmull path between left and right grip points.

Still plotting handlebar geometry...

Mirroring the brake lever to the right side with its own joint and master cylinder box, plus small mirror stalks with ellipsoid heads. Now I'm positioning the headlight forward of the fork tubes, working out the fork's axis geometry to place it at the right depth and height.

Modeling the headlight as a cylindrical housing with a glowing cyan lens disc on the front, attached so it rotates with the steering bone, with support rods connecting the fork legs to the bucket sides. Then I'm laying out the two fork legs as rods running from the top tree down toward the headlight bracket points.

Working out the fork geometry: computing the stanchion and slider segments between the top tree, a midpoint, and the axle, including radii and colors for the upper chrome and lower dark sections, plus the axle shaft spanning between the leg bases and matching hub/tire widths.

Now I'm placing the triple trees - the top clamp box oriented along the fork's direction vector, computing that normalized axis for the box orientation, and figuring out where the bottom tree sits relative to the head tube's position.

I need to define the fork line parametrically along its unit direction so I can place the head tube, triple trees, and steer tube rod at consistent points along it, then work out the fork stanchion positions extending from the top clamp down to the leg mounts.

Now I'm placing the slider tubes toward the axle, verifying endpoint coordinates match the wheel geometry, and adding small details like boots, bands, and rings around the fork legs for visual texture. I'm also positioning the brake caliper and rotor relative to the front axle and slider.

For the front wheel assembly, I'm planning the fender attachment via stays connecting to the fork legs, then adding spokes. For the rear, I'm figuring out the axle caps, brake rotor placement on one side, and a belt pulley with teeth detail on the other side, using steel material with orange accents.

Now I'm working out the primary drive belt geometry: a pulley at the engine output and a larger pulley at the rear wheel, connected by two tangent rods representing the top and bottom edges of the belt, with the belt given a defined width to look visually accurate.

I'm also reconsidering the frame geometry since the chain stays and the belt could overlap in width -- I need to narrow the stay spacing so they sit inside the tire width rather than colliding with the belt run.

Now I'm placing chain and seat stays running from the frame down toward the rear axle, checking they clear the belt and fender widths, and adding rear axle hub caps as small cylinders near x=±0.13.

I'm skipping the sissy bar since the geometry keeps intersecting the fender, and instead working out placement for the taillight on the fender's rear end, calculating the angular position and resulting y/z coordinates for a glowing red box plus reflectors.

I'm adding a small license plate below the taillight, using a plane with an orange border and simple text like "XR-76", positioned to clear the rear tire and fender end without clipping into the wheel.

Then I'm placing forward foot controls: cylindrical pegs mounted at the sides near the front, with a shift lever and brake pedal joint attached to the frame, checking positions clear the front tire and cylinder heads.

For the lighting, I'm working out cyan underglow placement—since paint can't actually glow, I'll need separate emissive glow parts positioned along the frame or engine cover edges rather than floating strips beneath the chassis.

I'm adding glow accents on the engine cover, wheel rims, headlight, and an orange-red taillight, while keeping the color palette under 64 total. For the tank I'm planning a painted scheme with orange base, white stripe, and dark lower section, and considering whether to use a decal chevron pattern versus a simple textured plane for reliability's sake.

Writing tank paint logic...

Still writing paint logic...

For the frame, I'll keep a gunmetal base with small weld-bead details at tube joints, using tiny torus rings as collars with an orange accent. To keep part counts manageable, I'm merging fin geometries that share a bone and color into a single transformed geometry instead of spawning dozens of separate parts.

Spokes and tread lugs stay as individual parts since they're structurally distinct, but I'm budgeting for roughly 300 total parts and keeping triangle counts low on merged tori and lugs. Now I'm setting up typed helper types and a builder instance before writing the box/cylinder helper closures inside the build function.

Writing helper functions...

Still writing helper functions...

Adding the torus geometry for the tire, then generating lug nut geometries arranged in a circular pattern around the wheel hub...

Now I'm merging the lug geometries into a single tread part colored slightly lighter, then working out the rim cylinder dimensions so it sits inside the tire's inner radius with a slight overlap into the tube, sketching a lathe profile for the rim barrel outline.

From the side you'd see the tire surface through its visible radii, with the inner hole revealing the rim face — so I can build the wheel as a dished mag-style disc: a rim lip torus in orange plus a flat gunmetal face disc covering the hole, maybe with cut spokes for detail.

Working out the geometry: a full disc at x=0 colored dark gunmetal, chrome/orange spoke rods offset slightly outward, an orange hub cylinder, and a glow-ring torus near the inner radius on both faces for visual richness. For the rear wheel with radius .26 and tube .10, the inner radius comes out to .16, and I'll place the lip rings at half the width times 0.5 outward from center.

Hub length needs to extend beyond the rim for an axle cap, with chrome cylinder caps and an orange center. I'm now building the brake rotor using a lathe shape with a defined outline profile.

Placing rotors at specific x-offsets so they sit inside each tire's width without clashing with fork legs, checking the radius stays within the tire's inner clearance for both front and rear wheels.

The rear pulley sits outside the tire width so it's fully visible, and I'm sketching its lathe outline along with the belt positioned just outside the pulley flange.

For the belt sweep, I need to use a function returning a tapered box radius instead of a fixed ellipse, since the path runs mostly along the X axis. I'll place the primary cover and its pulley slightly forward and up from the rear pulley position.

Now I'm working through positioning to avoid collisions: the gearbox box sits behind at z≈-0.14, the output pulley spans roughly z -0.19 to -0.09, and the primary cover spans z -0.02 to 0.22, so they clear. I'm checking the crankcase box dimensions and position next to the gearbox box to make sure their z-spans don't overlap either.

Now I'm laying out the cylinder geometry: front cylinder base, direction tilted at 25°, with a core cylinder shape plus six cooling fin discs spaced along its length, topped by a head and valve cover.

Still placing engine parts... I'm defining the rear cylinder mirroring the front one, then positioning an air cleaner cylinder between them with chrome/orange detailing and turbine-style rings for visual texture.

Now I'm routing the exhaust pipes from each cylinder head, tracing a curved path from the front head's exhaust port downward and backward along the frame toward the rear.

I'm checking that the seat frame clears the saddle area, then tracing the pipe as it runs back toward the rear, verifying the spacing between the front and rear pipes stays wider than their combined radius so they don't intersect.

Adding exhaust tip geometry...

Checking overall proportions: total length comes to about 2.84m front to rear, which fits a chopper's typical 2.4-2.8m range. Now I'm positioning the seat loft on the frame, tracing the top tube slope down toward the rear fender area.

I spot a conflict — the top tube at that z-position would sit higher than the seat top, so I need to redefine the frame spine's curve to dip lower before reaching the seat tube, routing through intermediate points from the head down to the rear axle area. Then I'm checking where the tank sits on top of this adjusted spine to make sure its bottom edge still clears properly.

Working out tank cross-section stations...

Checking spine against tank boundaries at each z-slice: it mostly stays under or touches the tank with small gaps, so the frame geometry should read as plausible underneath the tank shape.

Now I'm working out the seat position, trying to set its y-center and height at each z-station so the seat cushion rests just above the spine without excessive gaps, roughly spanning from z=-0.62 to z=-0.12.

Adding chain stays from the crank, running a seat tube rod through the crankcase area (hidden geometrically), and routing the down tube from the head bottom to the engine, checking whether it clips through the front cylinder.

I'm checking clearance between the down tube and the front cylinder at several heights along its path, nudging the tube curve forward with a catmull spline so it stays clear of the cylinder radius at each sampled point.

Then I turn to smaller details: adding a glowing cyan speedo dial on the triple tree facing the rider, plus footpegs, pedals, and a kickstand joint positioned near the lower frame.

I'm checking that the kickstand's stowed position doesn't clash geometrically with the belt drive or exhaust pipes, so I try shifting it to the left side near the belt while keeping its pivot and rod clear of other components.

I'm checking the foot pad placement so it rests flush on the floor, then adding a bracket near the engine skid plate to avoid collisions with the stand pivot. I'm also placing the tank cap as a small chrome cylinder centered on top of the tank, aligning its height with the tank's loft geometry.

For the tank shape itself, I'm settling on a 12-sided loft for a smoother low-poly profile, rigged to the frame bone for weighting, and defining stations with position, width, and height. I'm applying the same loft approach to the seat with its own paint color and sides, then planning the tank decals as textures applied to the tank's sweep surface.

For the emblem decal placement, I'm figuring out the direction vectors and mirroring logic so the logo reads correctly on both left and right sides, working through the camera orientation math to make sure text direction matches what a viewer would naturally expect from each side.

Since text orientation is ambiguous with mirrored decals, I'll just skip text entirely and design a symmetric abstract emblem instead—something like a diamond with arrow shapes, using white and cyan accents against the orange tank body, avoiding any actual logos or lettering.

Simplifying the license plate to a plain monospace string, I'm now working through the mirror geometry and rear details: a glowing tail light box, fender racing stripes painted on via a procedural rule based on position and surface normal, matching front fender treatment, and solid gunmetal chassis grain. I'm also adding small bolt details by merging spheres at the stanchion clamps and engine covers.

Placing bolt rings around the primary cover, air cleaner, tree clamps, and headlight ring using small translated sphere meshes, then adding a torus rim with a glowing center to the primary cover for extra detail. I'm also considering rubber grip texture for the handlebars and skipping the front plate holder, then adding a thin glowing pinstripe sweep along both sides of the gas tank using emissive cyan rods.

I'm working out the orientation convention for the tube sweep angles so the pinstripe lines land correctly on the tank's sides rather than top or bottom, settling on roughly ±55 degrees given the loft direction runs rear-to-front along +z. I'm defining glow colors for cyan, headlight, and taillight accents, and deciding joints don't need an explicit role unless they're hinges, using the aim parameter to orient them properly in model space. Nothing needs to extend below the ground plane since the wheels define the tread line.

I'm now checking that several key y-coordinates — front and rear axle positions, kickstand pad, torus bottom — all line up correctly at or above zero, then shifting into writing the fork geometry helper that computes positions along the fork tube based on a normalized direction vector between the steering point and axle.

Writing fork geometry helpers...

Still placing fork hardware...

Still working through the geometry...

Checking where the fork crosses the fender height, I find the fork line at y=.552 sits at z=1.014, well inside the fender's .40 radius circle around the axle—meaning the fork stanchion geometrically intersects the fender arc. That's actually realistic, since real fenders mount directly onto the fork legs.

I'm widening the leg offset to ±0.095 so the stanchions clear the fender's half-width of .075, keeping a small gap, and I'll connect them with short mounting blocks or rods at specific angle points along the fender arc to simulate the attachment hardware.

Checking that the headlight sits comfortably above the fender's top edge without overlap, and confirming the axle and rotor dimensions on the front wheel line up with the leg spacing. Now I'm ready to start writing the actual geometry code, just need to settle on the fender arc length first.

Working out the front fender arc—starting it at the top near the headlight and sweeping forward 125° down to the wheel, then doing the same for the rear fender with a 90° sweep in the opposite rotational direction to keep it symmetric relative to the hub center.

Now I'm positioning the taillight and license plate at the rear fender's end point, checking clearances against the tire's rear extent so nothing clips, and adding a small bracket rod connecting the fender tip to the plate mount.

Working out the plate's text orientation so it reads correctly from behind — figuring out which local axis maps to the viewer's right when the camera sits behind the car looking forward.

Now I'm adding mirror stalks sprouting from the handlebar grips, with small ellipsoid mirror heads angled backward at the tips.

I'm sketching in the master cylinder box near the right grip and setting up the flat color palette—gunmetal tones, orange accents, and chrome highlights—to keep the whole model's shading consistent.

Now I'm writing the paint function for the seat, using a checkerboard pattern based on x and z coordinates to alternate between darker shades for a stitched leather look.

Then I'm planning the tank and fender paint functions, plus the frame tubes using a catmull-rom sweep bound to the frame bone with uniform weights, adding collar rings at tube junctions.

Now I'm setting up the imports for Three.js and the geometry merging utilities needed to assemble the final mesh.

Still writing imports...

I'm starting the build function by creating the builder instance and defining the main frame joint, then thinking through how to structure the rest of the parts in sequence, including a wheel helper function with configurable parameters.

Writing wheel geometry logic...

So the disc fills the tire hole like a dished plate, with rim lips added as small orange tori at offset positions, and I'm checking whether those lips stay visible given the tire's cross-section radius at that offset.

Now I'm working out spoke geometry, computing inner and outer radii off the hub and tire rim for each spoke angle.

Still adjusting wheel geometry...

Now I'm placing the brake calipers: orange boxes for the front caliper on the steering bone, and a rear caliper mounted to the frame near the rotor's edge, positioning it with a stay mount offset behind the hub.

I checked the geometry at the rear caliper location and confirmed it sits inside the tire's inner hole clearance, so it doesn't clip the tire mesh. Now I'm moving on to assembling the engine and the rest of the components.

I'm adding small fender struts connecting the rear fender to the axle, verifying their positions stay just outside the tire radius so they don't intersect it.

Now I'm working out the triple-tree assembly: a steering bone box, leg clamps using cylinders, and bolt positions computed by finding the normal vector perpendicular to the fork axis in the YZ plane so the bolts sit correctly on the tree surface.

Computing the head tube's position along the fork spine, then checking where the orange ring collars sit and working out the spine and down-tube start coordinates by projecting offsets off the frame axis.

Now I'm plotting a brake hose path from the lever to the caliper, trying to route it around the fork leg without clipping through it, adjusting the intermediate points so the curve clears the fork at each height.

Then I'm checking that it also stays clear of the front fender's profile at the point where their x-coordinates overlap, confirming the hose radius is thin enough and colored black.

With that confirmed, I'm moving on to compose the final geometry, planning a reusable bolts helper function that merges bolt geometries along a list of points with a given radius, color, and bone attachment.

Now I'm sketching a ring-placement helper for generating bolt circles around an axis, then laying out the primary cover's bolt positions, radius, and bolt size, along with the color constants and the engine's glow disc, cover cylinder, and ring torus geometry.

I'm checking the type signatures for the part, cylinder, glow, and lathe builder functions to make sure the direction and bone options line up correctly before writing the final file.

Designing the emblem and plate SVGs with angular accent shapes and a monospace bold text label for the decal textures.

Now I'm placing the tank decal on the sides and working out the tank cap position, adding a chrome cylinder cap with a small glow dot near the top where the tank tapers.

Skipping extra seat springs and piping for simplicity, I'm moving on to writing the engine helper function that computes cylinder directions and positions for the engine block geometry.

Writing engine cylinder code...

For the engine head I'm adding a cylinder core, a cover box with bolt details, and small chrome rods for spark plugs, picking tilt angles for the front and rear cylinder banks to get the classic V-twin splay.

Checking the box orientation against the direction vector to make sure the fin width and depth map correctly, then confirming fin radius doesn't clash badly with the cylinder spacing at the crank.

Now writing the exhaust pipe path coordinates...

I'm checking clearances — making sure the rear pipe's catmull curve, heat shield placement, and rider foot peg position don't collide with the pipe route near the base.

I'm positioning the right-side footpeg, mount rod, and brake pedal pivot so they clear the exhaust pipe geometry, keeping the pedal pad forward of the peg and leaving the left side with just a peg stub. Footboard bolt counts check out, so I'm moving on to finalizing the code.

Still checking the kickstand's clearance against the belt and primary cover, then placing its pivot and tip coordinates below the cover. I'm writing the full numeric values into the model code now, defining the steering, front wheel hinge, and handlebar lever joints with their pivot and aim points.

Now I'm mirroring the brake lever to the opposite side, finalizing the seat loft geometry, and wiring the tank sweep into the line and decal parts, plus adding an underglow bar and skid plate before writing out the complete file.
